title: The 10 Best Z-Wave Dimmer Switches
subtitle: In-wall dimmers for Z-Wave hubs, ranked from live Amazon data.
intro: We pulled the in-wall Z-Wave dimmers selling on Amazon, checked each listing, and scored them on rating, review volume, and features: 800 Series Long Range radios, 3-way support without add-on switches, and adjustable dimming. On/off switches are on our Z-Wave light switches page.

buyers_guide.q: Will a smart dimmer work with my LED bulbs?
buyers_guide.a: Only with bulbs marked dimmable, and even then some combinations flicker or buzz at low levels. Dimmers with an adjustable minimum brightness (sometimes called low-end trim) let you raise the bottom of the range until the flicker stops.
Smart dimmers list a maximum load, often around 150 W of LED and 600 W of incandescent. Add up the bulbs on the circuit. If you're close to the limit, pick a higher-rated model or split the load.

buyers_guide.q: Can I use a smart dimmer on a ceiling fan?
buyers_guide.a: No. Dimmers are for lights. Fans need a fan speed control or an on/off switch rated for motors.

buyers_guide.q: Do Z-Wave dimmers need a hub?
buyers_guide.a: Yes. They pair to a Z-Wave controller such as Home Assistant with a Z-Wave adapter, Hubitat, SmartThings with a Z-Wave hub, or Homey Pro. Smart speakers can't talk to Z-Wave directly.

buyers_guide.q: Do I need a neutral wire?
buyers_guide.a: Most smart switches need one because the electronics stay powered when the light is off. Open the box and look for a bundle of white wires tied together at the back. If it's there, you have a neutral. Older homes, especially those built before the mid-1980s, often don't. If yours doesn't, pick a switch listed as no-neutral.

buyers_guide.q: Will a smart switch work on a 3-way circuit?
buyers_guide.a: Only if it says so. A 3-way circuit controls one light from two switches. Some smart switches handle that on their own and keep the existing switch at the other end. Others need a matching add-on or companion switch, and some only work on single-pole circuits.

If you're comfortable replacing an ordinary switch, the job is similar: power off at the breaker, confirm it's dead with a tester, and match the wires. Check local code, and hire an electrician if the box is crowded, the wiring is aluminum, or you're not sure which wire is which.
